sources.title: Single-Tone Parameter Estimation from Discrete-Time Observations
sources.venue: IEEE Transactions on Information Theory 20(5), 591-598 (bibliographic record surfaced through CiNii Research)
sources.publication_status: Journal article metadata verified; peer-review status not independently established in accessed material
sources.access_level: Inaccessible (primary DOI/PDF attempts failed); secondary indexed excerpts only
sources.content_locator: No direct primary-paper passage used. Clarkson full text S1 lines 71-108 summarizes its periodogram-MLE method and coarse FFT/fine-search implementation; do not treat this as direct inspection of S3.

findings.claim: For a single stationary complex sinusoid in white Gaussian noise with unknown phase, the periodogram maximum is the ML frequency estimate; a coarse FFT followed by a local fine search is a practical approximation. Clarkson's comparison reports statistical efficiency for large sample count or SNR, while showing that O(N) phase-difference alternatives can lose efficiency outside their favorable SNR/sample-count region.
findings.support_locator: S1 lines 71-108; lines 211-238. Direct S3 paper was inaccessible; S1 explicitly attributes the likelihood result to Rife and Boorstyn.
findings.decision_implication: Keep a bounded coarse-to-fine likelihood fit as a strong acquisition/reference candidate against the current short phase-difference estimator. Compare finite-error tails, not only RMS or the local CRLB; a finite uncertainty estimate alone does not expose missed-peak/outlier probability.
findings.assumptions: One tone; stationary frequency over fit aperture; complex sinusoid; independent complex white Gaussian noise; no unresolved interferer or envelope violation.
findings.applicability_gap: The task has real generated helper tone, payload/auxiliary activity, possible ramps/drift, finite chunks, and calibrated false publications; cited simulations and model do not validate those conditions or the proposed 95% target.
findings.next_discriminator: On matched tone-present and absent captures, sweep the stated offsets and reference levels; compare acquisition latency, absolute-error tail, missed/false publications, and empirical interval coverage for FFT-seeded fit versus current tracker, stratified by clean/noisy, payload activity, and chunk size.

findings.claim: Weighted phase-difference/Kay-style estimators provide an O(N)-time, O(1)-memory route that avoids explicitly unwrapping every sample phase, but the accessible comparative study reports original Kay-window bias near the argument branch point. Its simple recursive phase-difference reference can set a local branch point before applying the weighted estimate, retaining linear complexity; estimator efficiency still depends on SNR/sample count and model fit.
findings.support_locator: S1 lines 109-140 and 176-210; S1 lines 232-238. S2 abstract independently states Kay's estimator performs well versus ML at moderately high SNR for a single complex sinusoid in complex white Gaussian noise.
findings.decision_implication: This is a plausible lightweight refinement/alternative to fixed-lag short phase differences, especially if CPU/memory bounds dominate. Explicitly test wrap/branch behavior at both offset extremes and low reference level before interpreting small covariance as calibrated confidence.
findings.assumptions: Single complex sinusoid; white Gaussian noise; phase increments remain locally trackable; model's recursive initial estimate is good enough to position the branch point.
findings.applicability_gap: Source uses normalized radian/sample and synthetic trials; it does not cover real-valued/conjugate ambiguity, the helper envelope or adjacent payload, nonwhite interference, frequency evolution, or empirical uncertainty calibration.
findings.next_discriminator: At identical sample supports, compare current short-lag estimator with a recursively branch-tracked weighted phase-difference fit, focusing on offsets near each wrap boundary, 24 dB-Hz, onset/ramp, and sudden drift; log failures and interval coverage as well as error.

findings.claim: The candidate estimator comparison itself must include threshold behavior and model failures: Clarkson's simulations show high-SNR efficiency does not establish low-SNR behavior, and the original Kay-window phase method can have large branch-point bias. CRLB-like bounds are conditional on the paper's tone/noise model and do not certify an engineering uncertainty interval or presence decision.
findings.decision_implication: Validation should report per-capture empirical quantiles/coverage, acquisition-time distribution, outlier/decline counts, and absent-control admissions. Separate any frequency fit from presence qualification and retain all nonpublications as the task requires.
findings.assumptions: Repeated controlled captures represent the target envelope of amplitude, noise, interference, onset, drift, and chunk delivery; timestamps and truth are accurate.
findings.applicability_gap: The sources do not prescribe a confidence calibration procedure for this receiver or establish sufficient capture count for the invented 95% target.
findings.next_discriminator: Use seeded, paired captures with known injected frequency, matched absent controls, and a held-out condition set; score empirical interval coverage and false admission separately from conditional error on successful publications.

findings.claim: A frequency-rate model is a distinct candidate if matched captures show smooth within-aperture drift: published work on joint frequency/rate maximum-likelihood estimation exists, but this search found only third-party metadata/abstract snippets and could not inspect primary content. It is not evidence that a drift model is needed or superior here.
findings.support_locator: Search results only for Abatzoglou, IEEE Transactions on Aerospace and Electronic Systems, 1986, DOI 10.1109/TAES.1986.310805; primary paper not accessed, so no technical claim beyond existence/title is relied upon.
findings.decision_implication: Do not select a higher-order model from this evidence. First determine whether constant-frequency fits show residual curvature or held-out error correlated with aperture duration; preserve conditional uncertainty for whichever evolution model is tested.
findings.assumptions: Drift is smooth and adequately represented by a linear frequency-rate model within the aperture; additional parameters can be identified at the available SNR.
findings.applicability_gap: No primary technical passage or direct peer-review evidence accessed; search result models may not match helper-tone dynamics.
findings.next_discriminator: On matched captures, compare constant-frequency and frequency-rate residuals and held-out prediction error across multiple aperture lengths; reject the added parameter if it does not improve tail error/coverage without destabilizing fits.

rejected_or_redundant: Generalized Kay estimator and Kalman tracking records were discovered but not pursued after primary full-text evidence on periodogram ML and phase-difference methods covered the immediate estimator decision. Their model-specific results would not materially change the first matched discriminator.

Rife-Boorstyn 1974 and Kay 1989 are IEEE journal articles, but the available pages do not independently establish peer-review policy; direct Rife full text was inaccessible and Kay was abstract-only. No direct content claims are attributed to inaccessible passages.
The 1976 multiple-tone paper scan was inaccessible. Multi-tone interference treatment therefore remains a validation gap rather than a researched algorithm recommendation.
Abatzoglou frequency-rate paper was not opened: only secondary snippets were found and budget ended. No claim of its performance or applicability is made.
unresolved: Whether actual helper captures are sufficiently stationary within independent apertures or maintain phase across dwells; the supplied comments state contracts/assumptions but not measured behavior.
Whether 24 dB-Hz and the stated chunk delivery permit the proposed time/error target; none of these publications evaluates this receiver geometry or target.
How auxiliary activity and the real capture's conjugate-image/sideband ambiguity affect the competing estimators.
Whether any reported uncertainty can achieve calibrated >=95% coverage with useful finite frequency-only publications while absence controls remain rejected.

escalation_ready: Sol/Astra can decide whether to add a matched coarse-to-fine periodogram/ML baseline and recursively branch-tracked phase-difference comparator to the smallest next receiver discriminator. The evidence supports testing these as distinct options, not choosing an architecture or accepting the invented target. Include present/absent controls, offsets and levels, ramps/drift, auxiliary activity, both chunk sizes, coverage and tail statistics. The user-provided excerpts remain the only evidence for project contracts/runtime seams; no project execution or measurement was performed.
